items.title: Sifuna accuses Ruto administration of failing Kenyans in Diaspora, pledges better consular services
items.summary: NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 22 – Linda Mwananchi party leader Edwin Sifuna has accused President William Ruto’s administration of neglecting Kenyans living abroad, pledging sweeping improvements in consular services and stronger government support for citizens in the diaspora if his political camp assumes pow
items.text:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 22 – Linda Mwananchi party leader Edwin Sifuna has accused President William Ruto’s administration of neglecting Kenyans living abroad, pledging sweeping improvements in consular services and stronger government support for citizens in the diaspora if his political camp assumes power.
Sifuna said the current administration had failed to match the financial contribution of Kenyans abroad with efficient public services, leaving many struggling to access basic documentation and government assistance despite billions of shillings remitted home.
He singled out the Kenyan Embassy in Washington, saying understaffing and bureaucratic inefficiencies had subjected citizens to prolonged delays in accessing essential consular services, including national identity cards.
Speaking during the opening of Linda Mwananchi’s first international office in New Jersey, Sifuna said his previous engagements with Kenyans across the United States had exposed deep-seated dissatisfaction with the government’s handling of diaspora affairs.
He said Kenyans living abroad had increasingly felt abandoned by a government that readily benefits from their remittances but fails to provide adequate support when they need assistance.
“Kenyans living abroad do not feel that their government is there for them as much as they are there for their country. The resources you remit through hard labour are not commensurate with the level of services you receive,” he said.
Sifuna recalled visiting Texas, Houston, Maryland and Washington during a 2024 trip to the US, where he said he encountered widespread complaints over the inadequacy of consular services and the government’s apparent indifference to diaspora concerns.
He cited the limited staffing at the Washington embassy, claiming that the facility had only one legal counsellor, a situation he said contributed to delays in delivering basic services.
The Nairobi Senator argued that Kenya’s diplomatic missions should be measured by their ability to serve citizens rather than the number of embassies established abroad.
He called for a deliberate redistribution of consular resources to areas with substantial Kenyan populations, saying the government should prioritise accessibility and efficiency over the symbolic expansion of diplomatic missions.
“Rather than opening embassies in Europe just to feel good, consular support services should be deployed efficiently where large concentrations of Kenyans actually reside,” he said.
Sifuna also accused the Ruto administration of failing in its responsibility to protect Kenyans caught up in international conflicts, citing citizens who allegedly ended up fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
As a member of the Senate Defence Committee, he said he had raised the plight of missing Kenyans and those reportedly held as prisoners of war in Ukraine, but criticised Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi for failing to provide definitive answers to distressed families.
He claimed Mudavadi had sought to defer the matter until January when he appeared before the committee, prolonging the uncertainty surrounding the fate of the affected Kenyans.
Sifuna said expectations had been high that President Ruto’s visit to Russia would yield a diplomatic breakthrough, particularly a deal to secure the release and repatriation of Kenyans caught up in the conflict.
However, he expressed disappointment that the visit did not produce the anticipated announcement, arguing that the protection and welfare of Kenyan citizens abroad should rank among the government’s foremost responsibilities.
He contrasted Kenya’s response with that of other countries which deploy aircraft and naval vessels to evacuate their nationals from conflict zones, saying Nairobi must demonstrate similar commitment to the safety of its citizens.
The Linda Mwananchi leader said his political movement intended to pursue a more responsive diaspora policy, with the New Jersey office marking the beginning of efforts to establish a structured presence among Kenyans living abroad.
He urged Kenyans across the US, including those in Houston, Washington DC and Seattle, to rally behind the movement, saying diaspora communities would have a greater role in shaping its political agenda.
Sifuna said the movement had retained key leadership positions, including secretaries for diaspora affairs and international affairs, to strengthen engagement and coordination with supporters outside Kenya.
He also pledged to introduce transparent mechanisms for diaspora participation, particularly in political fundraising and mobilisation, following complaints by some supporters who had contributed personal resources to previous campaigns but felt sidelined afterwards.
He said the movement would establish formal structures to ensure supporters understood how resources were being utilised and had clear channels through which to participate in political activities.
Sifuna maintained that Kenyans in the diaspora were equal stakeholders in the country’s future, insisting that their financial contribution, political opinions and electoral choices deserved recognition.
“The entire purpose of this visit is to listen to you. Your views matter, your contribution to the development of our country matters, and your vote matters,” he said.

items.text:
COP31: Fossil fuels still missing from draft deal at UN climate summit
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 22, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached
- The latest COP31 draft deal still fails to mention fossil fuels, raising the possibility the summit could end with no deal
- Fossil fuels are a major flashpoint at this year's summit, which comes amid soaring energy prices and tensions over the US-Israeli war with Iran
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22:
What we know about the latest COP31 draft deal
The third draft makes no mention of the words "fossil," "oil," "coal," or "phase out."
However, as in the second draft, the latest version retains a goal to boost electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, as well as efforts to expand the use of "clean energy."
The draft text also does not stipulate that the "35-by-35" electrification target should be met using renewable energy sources.
It also urges countries to "accelerate" carbon capture and storage — a controversial technology backed by the fossil fuel industry.
Fossil fuels still missing in latest COP31 draft deal
Welcome back to our coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.
The latest, and potentially final, version of the deal still makes no explicit mention of fossil fuels.
It does refer to a 2023 agreement that committed the world to transitioning away from fossil fuels — but stops short of naming them directly.
The third and presumably final draft text to emerge from negotiations at COP31, which lacks any mention of fossil fuels or how to transition away from them, has been rejected by NGOs.
In a statement, Teresa Anderson, Climate Justice Lead at ActionAid International, said the people who will benefit most from the new "35-by-35" electrification targets and carbon capture "are the fossil fuel, nuclear, data and CCUS (carbon capture, use and storage) industries.
"This text will help elites to profit while leaving people in the dark," Anderson said.
Brandon Wu, AAUSA's Director of Policy and Campaigns, said: "Rich countries came to the COP31 talks with nothing to offer other than red lines.
"They put forward meaningless fossil fuel transition roadmaps that were nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy, then hypocritically blamed developing countries for failing to take action on phasing out fossil fuels.
“This is the behaviour of an arrogant bully who cares about nothing but himself and it is no way to have a proper negotiation. COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it’s because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise."
We're pausing our coverage
As COP31 extends into a second day of overtime, we are pausing our coverage.
In the early hours of Sunday, COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum informed delegates at a plenary that a third and "final" text would be sent to them for review.
He added that negotiators would have until 6:00 am (0400 GMT) "to come to us with agreement on the text" and that a closing plenary would then be convened at 9:00 am local time.
Stay tuned for more news in the coming hours.
IN DEPTH: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
The shift to green tech is already in full swing, including electric cars, electric buses, solar panels and heat pumps. But what is so electrifying about the latest wave of electrification?
Climate activist blames rich countries for COP failure
Harjeet Singh, the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign and strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, said that COP31 could be a failure due to a lack of funding.
"COP31 is stuck for one simple reason: money. Europe and other rich countries came to Antalya with empty pockets," he wrote in a statement shared with multiple reporters.
"They've spent two weeks pushing electrification targets and demanding more ambition from developing countries, while refusing to pay for any of it," he added.
Singh accused wealthy countries of blocking a just transition mechanism and of ignoring calls to increase funding for the Adaptation Fund and the Loss and Damage Fund.
"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he wrote.
The climate activist stressed that the reason this COP failed wasn't a lack of solutions. It was due to "a lack of money and a lack of will from those who caused this crisis," he said.
IN DEPTH: Why is carbon capture not moving faster?
Carbon capture technology works, but its real-world capabilities are nowhere near to moving the needle on climate change. So what's the hold-up?
IN DEPTH: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
Attacks on climate science and disinformation seem to be delaying key decisions as the UN climate talks draw to a close in Antalya.
IN DEPTH: Africa at COP31 — Will climate cash finally flow?
Leaders from Africa, one of the continents worst hit by climate change, have spent years lobbying for hundreds of billions of dollars to help adapt to the rising impacts of global warming.
The rest of the world relies on African nations for their abundant natural resources, many of them used in clean energy production.
Yet at COP31, wealthy nations have so far failed to commit to the financing needed to help developing nations make a just transition.
Read our report from DW's Kathy Wood.
Peru blames 'geopolitical divisions' for lack of COP31 progress
The head of Peru's delegation at COP31, Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, warned that the UN climate summit was unlikely to end with a concrete deal on climate financing or cutting fossil fuel use.

items.title: Ruto makes unannounced trip to Congo, abruptly ends Western tour
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – President William Ruto has cut short his Western Kenya development tour to attend a high-level diplomatic meeting in the Republic of Congo, where he is expected to hold talks with three other African leaders amid strained relations between Kenya and the Democratic Republic of
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – President William Ruto has cut short his Western Kenya development tour to attend a high-level diplomatic meeting in the Republic of Congo, where he is expected to hold talks with three other African leaders amid strained relations between Kenya and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
Ruto arrived in Oyo on Saturday, November 21, 2026, ahead of Sunday’s four-nation meeting convened by Republic of Congo President Denis Sassou-N’Guesso.
The President’s departure came just days after he launched an extensive development tour of Western Kenya, which began on Thursday, November 19, and was scheduled to run in two phases, concluding on December 1.
According to the programme outlined by Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, the first phase was due to run from November 19 to 24, before resuming on November 28 and ending on December 1.
Ruto’s abrupt departure therefore interrupted the first leg of the tour, which was expected to take him through Busia, Bungoma, Kakamega and Vihiga counties.
In a departure from his usual foreign travel arrangements, the President’s trip to Congo was not publicly announced by State House before his departure. His arrival was confirmed by the Congolese presidency in a statement posted on its official X account on Saturday.
“His Excellency Mr William Ruto, President of the Republic of Kenya, arrived in Oyo on Saturday, November 21, to take part in a high-level four-party meeting initiated by the Congolese President, His Excellency Mr Denis Sassou-N’Guesso,” the statement said.
The meeting will bring together Ruto, Sassou-N’Guesso, DRC President Félix Tshisekedi and Togo’s President of the Council, Faure Gnassingbé.
The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of strained relations between Nairobi and Kinshasa, with the four leaders expected to discuss regional relations and tensions in the Great Lakes region.
The disagreement between Kenya and the DRC escalated in December 2023 following the launch of the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), a political-military coalition associated with the M23 rebel movement, in Nairobi.
Kinshasa protested the event, accusing Kenya of providing a platform to a group it considers hostile. Nairobi, however, maintained that it could not restrict political expression.
Relations were further strained in October 2025 when Nairobi hosted a political gathering involving Congolese opposition figures, including former DRC President Joseph Kabila.
Gnassingbé’s participation adds a wider regional dimension to the meeting, given his involvement in African Union-led mediation efforts aimed at addressing tensions in the Great Lakes region.
Although the Congolese presidency confirmed the four-party meeting, it had not released a detailed agenda by Saturday.
Ruto’s trip comes at a politically sensitive moment, with his administration also seeking to consolidate support in Western Kenya ahead of the 2027 General Election. The President had been using the regional tour to launch development projects and rally residents behind his administration’s agenda.

items.title: Verstappen wins wild Las Vegas GP as Ferraris collide again
items.summary:
Las Vegas GP: Max Verstappen wins wild race as Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collide again
Max Verstappen wins wild Las Vegas Grand Prix; Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri claim double podium for McLaren after late Mercedes collapse saw George Russell and Kimi Antonelli drop back; Charle
items.text:
Las Vegas GP: Max Verstappen wins wild race as Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collide again
Max Verstappen wins wild Las Vegas Grand Prix; Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri claim double podium for McLaren after late Mercedes collapse saw George Russell and Kimi Antonelli drop back; Charles Leclerc penalised for causing collision with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton
Sunday 22 November 2026 05:56, UK
Max Verstappen produced a remarkable drive to win a wild Las Vegas Grand Prix that saw him withstand extreme pressure from George Russell and Kimi Antonelli before a late Mercedes collapse.
Pole-sitter Verstappen retained the lead at the start but the enormous power of a slipstream on the long straights of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit made it impossible for the leader to pull clear.
First Russell, and then later newly crowned world champion Antonelli were each able to pass Verstappen on several occasions but the Red Bull driver calmly retook the lead within a few corners every time, expertly managing the deployment of his power.

Russell, trying to pass his team-mate for second with three laps remaining, ran into a barrier after overshooting a corner and dropped down the order, before Antonelli appeared to suffer a deployment issue at the start of the final lap that allowed Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri to snatch a double podium for McLaren.
There was more unwanted drama for Ferrari as team-mates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collided again as they battled for sixth with 12 laps remaining, with the latter given a 10-second penalty by the stewards for causing the incident.
Pierre Gasly took fifth ahead of his team-mate Franco Colapinto to secure a major points haul for Alpine, with Hamilton recovering to seventh, having served a 10-second penalty himself earlier in the race for overtaking Norris off track.
Carlos Sainz snatched eighth from Russell on the run to the finish line to equal Williams' best result of the season, while Leclerc claimed the final point in 10th.

items.title: Kenyans in Diaspora offer Sifuna billions to build JKIA if he wins the presidency
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Kenyans living in the United States have challenged Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna to tap into the financial muscle of the diaspora to fund the expansion of Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), saying they are capable of mobilising resources for the project without invo
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Kenyans living in the United States have challenged Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna to tap into the financial muscle of the diaspora to fund the expansion of Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), saying they are capable of mobilising resources for the project without involving foreign investors.
The diaspora community said Kenyans abroad could pool their financial contributions and partner with the government to modernise the country’s main airport, cautioning Sifuna against pursuing another arrangement similar to the controversial deal with India’s Adani Group.
The proposal was presented by Kiemo Mohando, a Kenyan based in Columbus, Ohio, during a meeting with Sifuna and other Linda Mwananchi supporters in New Jersey on Saturday.
Mohando said Kenyans abroad had demonstrated their financial capacity through billions of shillings sent home annually and could channel part of the resources towards financing major infrastructure projects.
He challenged the community to move beyond individual remittances and establish a coordinated funding arrangement that would allow them to participate directly in the country’s development.
“We can build the airport. Don’t look for another Adani. We can build an airport. We can reorganise ourselves, let’s partner with the government, let’s do the airport,” Mohando said.
He maintained that the diaspora’s collective financial strength could provide an alternative to expensive infrastructure financing arrangements, which often attract public scrutiny over their terms and long-term implications.
“You see how much money we sent to Kenya. Yes. It’s a lot of it’s billions, right? We can build the airport,” he said.
Mohando also called for mechanisms that would allow diaspora members to contribute directly to development institutions, arguing that such an arrangement would strengthen transparency and accountability in the use of funds.
His proposal comes against the backdrop of the contentious JKIA expansion plan that brought the government under pressure in 2024 after it sought to enter into a long-term concession arrangement with Adani Airport Holdings.
The Adani controversy
The proposed deal, estimated at $1.85 billion, was designed to facilitate the construction of a second runway and a new passenger terminal at JKIA, alongside improvements to existing airport infrastructure.
Under the proposal, Adani Airport Holdings would have financed the project in exchange for a 30-year concession to operate the airport, raising concerns over the potential transfer of control of a strategic national asset to a private company.
The arrangement sparked resistance from aviation workers, who feared job losses and changes to their employment terms, as well as questions over the procurement process, transparency and the financial obligations Kenya would assume.
The Law Society of Kenya and the Kenya Human Rights Commission challenged the proposal in court, arguing that the arrangement raised constitutional and public procurement concerns.
The controversy intensified in November 2024 when Gautam Adani, the conglomerate’s founder, and other executives were indicted in the United States over allegations of bribery and securities fraud linked to energy contracts in India. The allegations were denied and did not constitute a conviction.
On November 21, 2024, President William Ruto announced the cancellation of the proposed JKIA procurement process, citing new information from investigative agencies and international partners.
The decision also affected a separate proposed electricity transmission partnership involving Adani, effectively bringing the group’s major infrastructure ambitions in Kenya to an abrupt halt.
The collapse of the airport proposal left the government under pressure to identify alternative financing arrangements for JKIA’s expansion as demand for air travel and airport capacity continued to grow.
The diaspora proposal now introduces another option into the debate, with Mohando arguing that Kenyans abroad should be considered development partners rather than merely sources of remittances.
Sifuna courts diaspora backing
The meeting was part of Sifuna’s engagements with Kenyans in the United States, where he officially opened the first international office of the Linda Mwananchi Movement in New Jersey.
The Nairobi Senator used the occasion to criticise the government over what he described as persistent neglect of Kenyans living abroad, particularly in the delivery of consular services and protection of citizens caught up in international conflicts.
He argued that despite their substantial contribution to the economy, Kenyans in the diaspora continued to face bureaucratic hurdles when seeking government assistance.
Sifuna also called for stronger diaspora structures within the movement, saying Kenyans abroad should have a transparent platform through which they could contribute to political activities and participate in shaping the country’s future.
He said the visit was intended to listen to their concerns and establish lasting channels of engagement.
“The entire purpose of this visit is to listen to you. Your views matter, your contribution to the development of our country matters, and your vote matters,” Sifuna said.

items.text:
New draft deal aims to avert collapse of talks at climate summit
- Published
Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggled to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.
Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
And it includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
Countries were expected to reconvene at 09:00 local time (06:00GMT) to decide whether to approve a new deal.
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday. On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said. "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."
What has the issue been?
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".
France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
In the latest text the commitments to CCUS have been reduced, which may be enough to alleviate the EU's concerns.
For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
'We did not come here to beg'
One of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money - appears unresolved in the latest draft agreement.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

items.text:
Displaced Darfur families face volatile winter as Sudan aid cuts bite
Sudan’s displacement crisis could worsen with winter approaching.
Omdurman, Sudan – When Fatima Mohamed Haroun was displaced from West Darfur state at the start of Sudan’s war in 2023, she never imagined she would find herself caring for four of her grandchildren far from her home.
Haroun, who believes she is aged about 60, said her son went missing a year ago. His wife died after giving birth, leaving Haroun as the sole guardian of her four grandchildren.
Now living in a crumbling mudbrick building in al-Ghadir, north of Omdurman, in Khartoum state, she has received no humanitarian assistance since her displacement.
Without an income, it is only the goodwill of her neighbours that prevents Haroun and her grandchildren from starving. But every day is a battle to find food, water or medicine, and with winter fast approaching, proper shelter, warm clothes, and blankets for the children are another priority.
“I cannot work or earn money, so we depend on neighbours who occasionally give us food. But even our neighbours sometimes have nothing to eat. When they have no food, my grandchildren and I go to bed hungry,” she told Al Jazeera.
“We have no supplies to help us cope with the cold, not even blankets to keep us warm. We sleep on the ground with only the sky above us. The cold is severe, and the children are suffering. We appeal to the government and humanitarian organisations to provide food, blankets, covers and other basic necessities to help us endure the cold and protect our children.”
Temperatures can drop significantly in Omdurman during the winter, and at night al-Ghadir can be particularly cold due to its location close to mountainous areas. Displaced families living in temporary shelters here are especially vulnerable because they lack blankets, winter clothing and heating facilities.
The war in Sudan, which broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in April 2023, has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
Khartoum state, which was initially one of the epicentres of the war but is now relatively more stable, continues to host large numbers of people forced to flee their homes, particularly from southern and western Sudan where fighting is ongoing. Millions of people in areas such as Darfur have experienced or are at risk of horrific violence, forcing them to flee to other parts of Sudan or neighbouring countries where they live in horrendous conditions.
As of July 30, Khartoum state was hosting 414,252 internally displaced people, according to data from the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM).
Winter is expected to worsen conditions for families living in temporary shelters or unfinished buildings without adequate blankets and warm clothing.
Sudan has more than 8.5 million internally displaced people, according to DTM Sudan, with the IOM and the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) warning that millions are still without a roof over their heads and risk losing access to emergency shelters due to funding shortages.
About 15.4 million people in Sudan need emergency shelter and basic household items. The agencies said funding shortages mean humanitarian organisations can prioritise assistance for only 10 percent of those in need, leaving millions without support.
Fighting, general insecurity, drone attacks on civilian infrastructure and camps, as well as other logistical challenges were all obstructing aid deliveries, the agencies said. Less than half of the funding for Sudan’s 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires $2.9bn to assist 20.4 million people in need, had been received, forcing humanitarian agencies to scale back some services.
Abdelaziz Suleiman Ori, director of culture and information for the Darfur regional government, said his administration was monitoring the conditions for displaced people in host states, including Khartoum, and coordinating humanitarian assistance.
The regional government has drawn up a winter plan that includes blankets, clothing and food to respond to the impending crisis, but Ori acknowledged that available resources were so far insufficient.
“Since the outbreak of the war on April 15, Governor Minni Arko Minawi has dispatched humanitarian convoys from Port Sudan to el-Fasher, passing through Madani, Kosti and El Obeid. We are also in contact with international organisations and UN agencies to monitor the situation of displaced people in different states,” Ori told Al Jazeera.
“Our winter plan includes blankets, clothing, food and children’s necessities. But our resources are not enough to meet the needs of the large number of displaced people. We appeal to humanitarian partners to provide more support.”
Ori said that only a collective response – involving regional government, host states, local authorities and NGOs – can properly respond to the crisis.
“Responsibility for displaced people is shared between the regional government, host states, local communities and humanitarian organisations,” he said.
“We coordinate efforts, seek relief assistance and monitor their conditions with local authorities. We bear part of the responsibility, but need greater cooperation to ease their suffering.”
Kheira Matar Hassan, a resident of Darfur, passed through Renk, Rabak and Khartoum at the start of the war before settling in al-Ghadir camp in 2023. She became separated from her husband when he went looking for work in a gold mining area in Chad at the same time.
She has received no word from him since he disappeared and has been left alone to support their seven children. They live in a dilapidated home built of bricks and mud bricks with damaged areas covered with cloth and plastic sheeting.
Hassan said she has received no support from the government or NGOs, and to support her children, she washes and irons clothes for families in the area, earning just enough

items.text:
Fossil fuel impasse pushes COP31 climate talks into second day of overtime
COP31 President Murat Kurum asks negotiators to consider a last-minute proposal in attempt to reach an agreement.
Turkish officials have asked negotiators at the COP31 climate summit to consider a last-minute proposal as talks stretched into a second day of overtime over the fossil fuels issue.
“We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told a late-night plenary session on Saturday.
Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, said the conference would reconvene later on Sunday morning to approve the deal.
The latest text was not immediately made public, and it was unclear if negotiators had received the wording overnight, which would give nations only a few hours to submit objections and changes.
An earlier draft had drawn strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels, the largest contributors to climate change.
Kurum said he believed concerns around fossil fuels had been addressed, as had those around helping developing countries finance their adaptations to climate change.
The new text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is leading the talks; Turkiye, which is hosting the meeting; and nearly 200 delegations from many of the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.
Delegations had until 03:00 GMT on Sunday to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 06:00 GMT to begin approving it.
The summit’s agreement is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heatwaves, floods and other disasters.
An opening draft from Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.
Key issues that slowed down the agreement included how much effort countries should make to wean themselves off fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and gas.
Other issues included whether to encourage industrial carbon capture and storage of pollutants, as well as whether ramping up electricity should only be done with renewables, such as wind and solar, or also involve other sources like natural gas and coal.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions.
The two-week talks in the Turkish city of Antalya were due to end on Friday.
In a letter sent on Saturday to this year’s cohosts, Turkiye and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs” the UN has ever held.
The letter stated there were only hours left “to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations”.
In the lead-up to these talks, the United Nations said the world would likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

items.text:
Eleven killed in burst of violence during Mexican cartel leader’s capture
Seven alleged cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed in the operation to arrest Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
The operation to capture Mexican cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores in the country’s Sinaloa state has left at least 11 people dead.
Mexico’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed in the overnight operation.
Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was captured on Friday and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after hours-long violence involving a firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight, roadblocks and burning trucks in the city of Guasave.
Two other men were also captured and flown to Mexico City. The ministry identified them as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, an alleged financial operator of the cartel. Both were also flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.
Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, climbed the ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the boss of his own group, the Meza-Flores transnational criminal organisation.
He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos”, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which the United States designated as a “foreign terrorist organization” last year.
The US wanted Meza Flores for trafficking drugs to the country and offered a $5m reward for information leading to his arrest.
Residents terrified
The firefight in Guasave broke out about 7pm on Friday (02:00 GMT on Saturday), according to residents. Military helicopters and drones were soon flying overhead, with helicopters opening fire on key locations across the city.
Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below.
Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4am (11:00 GMT) on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to discuss the case.
While a tense calm has settled over Guasave since the operation, experts warned that picking off cartel bosses could set off more waves of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring factions.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on cartels and has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors. Homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.
The US Drug Enforcement Administration commended Mexican authorities, as did Washington’s ambassador to Mexico.
“Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together,” US Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post.

items.text:
Overturned boat carrying mourners to funeral kills at least 24 in Nigeria
Police say the boat driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
A boat believed to be carrying hundreds of attendees to a funeral has overturned in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, according to authorities.
The overcrowded vessel capsized on Friday in Bayelsa State after a mechanical failure while travelling from the communities of Ayama to Ukubie, according to police.
“So far, 24 bodies have been recovered from the scene of the incident, while search and rescue operations are ongoing,” Manzo Ezekiel, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency, said on Saturday.
Rescue and search operations were continuing, he added.
Two children were among the four bodies initially recovered from the water on Friday, police said at the time, adding that 24 people were rescued, with 19 treated at a local clinic and five taken to hospital in the state capital.
Police did not say how many people were on board, but some residents told the Reuters news agency there were at least 300.
Police said the driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
According to a statement from the Bayelsa State Police Command, the accident occurred at the river junction between the Oweikorogha and Otuan communities, in the state’s Southern Ijaw district.
The boat that capsized was travelling “for a burial ceremony”, the statement also said, adding that police are “coordinating efforts with local divers and other responders”.
Such boat accidents are common on Nigeria’s busy rivers and waterways, often caused by overloaded vessels, poor maintenance, or failure to comply with safety regulations.
A similar incident occurred in August, when at least 51 people died after a boat sank in northwest Nigeria’s Sokoto State. In another incident, in January, at least 26 people drowned after a boat ferrying people from Jigawa to Yobe State capsized.

items.text:
Displaced Palestinians protest as Israeli air strikes continue in Gaza
Israeli forces continue to destroy residential buildings as part of a ‘gradual displacement’ policy, a Gaza mayor says.
Hundreds of displaced Palestinians have protested as Israeli forces continue to destroy residential buildings in Gaza, beyond the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire.
Al Jazeera journalist Moath al-Kahlout, reporting from Gaza’s Deir el-Balah, said displaced Palestinians who live in the area near the “Yellow Line” gathered on Saturday to demonstrate against Israel’s intensifying air strikes.
The “Yellow Line” separates Israeli- and Hamas-controlled areas in Gaza since the “ceasefire” signed in October 2025.
“More than 500 housing units have been destroyed in less than a month,” said Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir-el Balah’s Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera.
“This is part of what appears to be a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement aimed at forcing residents out of their camp and destroying as many homes as possible,” Musleh said.
Gaza’s Ministry of Public Works and Housing says 350,000 families are homeless after Israeli attacks destroyed 80 percent of the enclave’s homes.
Meanwhile, flooding in recent weeks devastated temporary tent housing, the ministry said.
The original “Yellow Line”, established under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, marked the area to which Israeli forces initially withdrew. They were expected to make further withdrawals gradually, but instead seized more territory.
“If we go back to October 2025, when the ceasefire was signed, the ‘Yellow Line’ was much further east,” al-Kahlout said.
Now, nearly two-thirds of Gaza is under Israeli army control or subject to access restrictions.
Rising death toll
Israeli attacks killed at least four Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday, including three who died when an Israeli drone struck a van delivering food aid to displaced people in Gaza City.
In the past 48 hours, Israeli strikes killed at least nine people, taking the death toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,661, according to the latest report from Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
The ministry said 55 Palestinians were wounded in the past 48 hours, putting the total number of the wounded since October 2025 at 6,062.
More than 100 remains recovered
Gaza’s Civil Defence said on Saturday that its crew members recovered the bodies and remains of 129 people from 39 homes and other Israeli-destroyed buildings in the Nuseirat refugee camp, az-Zawayda and Deir el-Balah in central Gaza.
Rami al-Aidi, Civil Defence director in central Gaza, said 233 people had been reported missing beneath the rubble of those buildings.
The 53-day operation marked the conclusion of the second phase of a recovery project in central Gaza funded by the International Committee of the Red Cross.
Gaza’s Civil Defence said in October that about 8,000 bodies remained under the rubble across the enclave, including about 4,000 in Israeli-controlled areas. The agency warned that recovery could take eight to 10 years with the equipment available.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special f
items.text:
Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
- Published
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
Eight people in total were arrested, including Meza Flores' second-in-command, who is also his cousin, and his brother-in-law, who is the group's financial operator, the secretariat added.
Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa.
Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash.
The US Consulate General in the city of Hermosillo said it was "monitoring reports of ongoing security operations, armed clashes, road blockades, and vehicle fires that occurred overnight in Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave, and Navolato" following the arrest of Meza-Flores.
It advised US citizens to remain alert for potential violence in the area and for residents to remain sheltered in place.
When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

COP31: UN Climate summit runs into second day of overtime
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 22, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached
- Peru blames 'geopolitical divisions' for lack of COP31 progress
- After a draft climate deal stripped all mentions of coal, oil, and gas, nations are bracing for another long night of negotiations
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22:
We're pausing our coverage
As COP31 extends into a second day of overtime, we are pausing our coverage.
In the early hours of Sunday, COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum informed delegates at a plenary that a third and "final" text would be sent to them for review.
He added that negotiators would have until 6:00 am (0400 GMT) "to come to us with agreement on the text" and that a closing plenary would then be convened at 9:00 am local time.
Stay tuned for more news in the coming hours.
IN DEPTH: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
The shift to green tech is already in full swing, including electric cars, electric buses, solar panels and heat pumps. But what is so electrifying about the latest wave of electrification?
Climate activist blames rich countries for COP failure
Harjeet Singh, the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign and strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, said that COP31 could be a failure due to a lack of funding.
"COP31 is stuck for one simple reason: money. Europe and other rich countries came to Antalya with empty pockets," he wrote in a statement shared with multiple reporters.
"They've spent two weeks pushing electrification targets and demanding more ambition from developing countries, while refusing to pay for any of it," he added.
Singh accused wealthy countries of blocking a just transition mechanism and of ignoring calls to increase funding for the Adaptation Fund and the Loss and Damage Fund.
"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he wrote.
The climate activist stressed that the reason this COP failed wasn't a lack of solutions. It was due to "a lack of money and a lack of will from those who caused this crisis," he said.
IN DEPTH: Why is carbon capture not moving faster?
Carbon capture technology works, but its real-world capabilities are nowhere near to moving the needle on climate change. So what's the hold-up?
IN DEPTH: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
Attacks on climate science and disinformation seem to be delaying key decisions as the UN climate talks draw to a close in Antalya.
IN DEPTH: Africa at COP31 — Will climate cash finally flow?
Leaders from Africa, one of the continents worst hit by climate change, have spent years lobbying for hundreds of billions of dollars to help adapt to the rising impacts of global warming.
The rest of the world relies on African nations for their abundant natural resources, many of them used in clean energy production.
Yet at COP31, wealthy nations have so far failed to commit to the financing needed to help developing nations make a just transition.
Read our report from DW's Kathy Wood.
Peru blames 'geopolitical divisions' for lack of COP31 progress
The head of Peru's delegation at COP31, Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, warned that the UN climate summit was unlikely to end with a concrete deal on climate financing or cutting fossil fuel use.
Garrido Sanchez lamented that the outcome "would be very limited."
He reiterated how "geopolitical divisions" were stopping any final deal from mentioning reducing reliance on oil, gas and coal.
The Peruvian delegate singled out major oil producers, such as Gulf Arab states and Russia, as showing significant opposition.
He noted that while Latin American neighbor Panama had also signaled objection to including the term fossil fuels in the final text, Peru was "not so radical" and is keen to attract investment to "ensure our energy security" through renewables.
China throws weight behind '35-by-35' pledge
China has backed a plan proposed by COP host Turkey to raise global electricity demand to 35% by 2035 — up from the current 20%.
In a joint statement with Australia, which is leading negotiations between almost 200 nations at the COP31 summit in Turkey, Beijing said it welcomes "growing international ambition and cooperation ... to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 on a voluntary basis."
The statement goes on to highlight the benefits the transition can bring for the economy, jobs, energy security, public health and households.
The two partners also "acknowledge the importance of inclusive climate action that ensures no one is left behind," the text continued.
Dozens of countries, including EU states, Japan, South Korea and Canada, have so far signaled support for the voluntary goal, which aims to boost clean energy use.
Yet, environmental groups have warned that the draft text doesn't stipulate the use of solar, wind and other renewable energy sources, which could allow power plants using natural gas and coal to be included.
COP31: What to expect today
Good morning, and welcome back to DW's coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries worked through the night to finalize a deal, after a draft text dropped all mention of fossil fuels — the leading cause of climate change.
COP31, being held in the Mediterranean city of Antalya, was due to wrap up on Friday, but has run over time amid deep divisions over fossil fuels.

items.summary:
MADRID -- Real Madrid supersub Carlos Espí said his 85th-minute winner against Celta Vigo was his "most special" goal yet for the club after earning his team all three points at the Bernabéu on Saturday.
Celta's Pablo Durán put the visitors ahead after just six minutes, before a late rally saw Jude
items.text:
MADRID -- Real Madrid supersub Carlos Espí said his 85th-minute winner against Celta Vigo was his "most special" goal yet for the club after earning his team all three points at the Bernabéu on Saturday.
Celta's Pablo Durán put the visitors ahead after just six minutes, before a late rally saw Jude Bellingham level for Madrid, and then Espí -- who was introduced on 79 minutes by coach José Mourinho -- score from close range, after Vinícius Júnior's cross, to seal a 2-1 victory.
- Madrid chief Pérez: "outrageous" that LaLiga president Tebas hasn't resigned
- Hunter: Has Vini Jr. finally put summer transfer saga behind him? Real Madrid need him at his best
Espí, 21, has played just 44 minutes for Madrid in LaLiga this season but he's now scored three, crucial goals to secure victories against Espanyol, Elche and Celta, as well as netting in the club's 4-3 Champions League comeback win away at Roma.
"I think it's the most special," Espí told reporters on Saturday, when asked about his first goal scored in front of the Bernabéu crowd.
"Honestly, it's a day I'll never forget ... I can't even count how many times I've dreamed of scoring here, celebrating with the fans, and hearing them chant my name."
Espí said coach Mourinho was "euphoric" after his late winner, and described meeting Rafael Nadal post-match, after the tennis legend was voted onto Madrid's board of directors earlier on Saturday.
"I went over to see [Nadal], and he was very proud of me," Espí said. "Having a legend like Rafa Nadal there, talking to me, it made me incredibly happy."
Mourinho cited the return from the international break as a factor in Madrid's lackluster first-half performance, which saw them trail at halftime.
"If you look at the big teams that played today: Arsenal didn't win, [Manchester] City didn't win, Chelsea didn't win, Bayern [Munich] didn't win," Mourinho said. "It's difficult."
Mourinho confirmed that Vinícius -- who he brought off the bench after 57 minutes on Saturday -- would start in Madrid's Champions League game with PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.
The coach also revealed why Espí is unlikely to start many games alongside first-choice center forward Kylian Mbappé.
"It's possible, but when we lose the ball, I -- on the touchline -- would have to run onto the pitch during the transition, and clatter someone on the opposing team," Mourinho joked.
"Playing with two pure forwards means your wingers have to be very capable of defending in central areas. And that wouldn't be Vinícius, for sure. Arda [Güler] might do it a bit, Brahim [Díaz] a bit, but given the characteristics of our wingers, we aren't built to play in a traditional 4-4-2."

- Raya exits with injury as Arsenal held by Newcastle: 'Never good news'

Home defeats to big rivals. Injuries to key players. One of the worst defenses in the Premier League.
Another crisis might be unfolding at Chelsea, just a few months into Xabi Alonso's tenure.
- Raya exits with injury as Arsenal held by Newcastle: 'Never good news'
- Man City at a crossroads as a shell of themselves
- VAR review: Should Haaland's goal vs Fulham have been disallowed
"We're in a fragile moment," Alonso said Saturday after seeing his team overrun in a 4-1 home loss to Leeds, who hadn't won at Stamford Bridge this century.
"We need to be tougher," he added. "It's something mandatory in this competition.
Already without major players in striker João Pedro and defender Maxence Lacroix because of injuries, Chelsea fell apart against Leeds following the enforced withdrawal of Moisés Caicedo in the 22nd minute after the Ecuador midfielder landed awkwardly on his back while making a challenge.
Despite going ahead within three minutes through Emmanuel Emegha on his first start, Leeds equalized almost immediately through Noah Okafor and dominated the second half, scoring through Dominic Calvert-Lewin -- via the penalty spot -- Okafor again and then U.S. midfielder Brenden Aaronson.
Leeds -- whose rivalry with Chelsea dates back to the 1960s and early '70s -- last beat the London club away in 1999. Less than a month ago, Tottenham won at Stamford Bridge for the first time since 2018. Before the international break, Chelsea lost 1-0 at Sunderland, which started that match in last place.
Chelsea, one of the biggest spenders in Europe in recent seasons, has tumbled toward midtable and are putting in lethargic performances even though the team doesn't have the hindrance of European competition this season.
"After we lost Moises, we lost completely the momentum," Alonso said. "Until then we were doing OK, but from that moment they started believing and we started not believing. After that, we never got the good feeling and were not able to come from the pressure. It completely changed.
"I'm not feeling [let down]. We do it as a team, as [a] collective. We need to support each other. We need to find solutions to do better because this will happen. There were moments that we were not competing at the level required. But the physicality, the duels, it's not the only explanation. The mentality part we can do better."
Chelsea has now conceded 20 goals in 11 games, with only last-place Crystal Palace and promoted teams Ipswich and Coventry letting in more.
Information from The Associated Press and PA contributed to this report.

items.title: Milan boss Amorim heaps praise on Pulisic: 'The player we cannot replace'
items.summary:
AC Milan head coach Ruben Amorim has heaped praise on Christian Pulisic, calling him "the player we cannot replace."
The 28-year-old is in sparkling form, having scored three goals in two games for the United States men's national team -- including a stunning bicycle kick -- and three in four in Ser
items.text:
AC Milan head coach Ruben Amorim has heaped praise on Christian Pulisic, calling him "the player we cannot replace."
The 28-year-old is in sparkling form, having scored three goals in two games for the United States men's national team -- including a stunning bicycle kick -- and three in four in Serie A prior to the international break.
"I can tell you today that Pulisic, maybe, is the player that we cannot replace," Amorim told a news conference ahead of Milan's game against Frosinone on Sunday.
"The characteristics of turning between the lines, we don't have another Pulisic. There are some moments in Europe, in this last schedule, we had to save -- a little bit -- Pulisic.
"There is nothing that I can say better than saying that Pulisic has some characteristics that, if we don't have it on the pitch, the team feels a lot that Pulisic is not there. From that, you can understand how important Pulisic is for us.
"He's not that kind of guy that speaks a lot, but [he] speaks on the pitch, without speaking. He wants the ball all the time and you can feel it against Genoa. If you see all the plays, Pulisic is the guy that pulls the team up. Him and [Adrien] Rabiot."
The former Borussia Dortmund and Chelsea winger has been with the Italian club since 2023 and recently signed a new deal through 2031.
"I think it helps any player to feel the confidence from the club," Amorim said on Saturday.
"I think [that] was clear [when] the club showed him a new contract. That helps always a player."

The Portuguese coach added: "When he was not playing [at the beginning of this season], I said 'Pulisic is really important for us.'
"But we cannot forget the injuries, the way we need to build the player in order to [suit] the context."
Milan sit in fifth place in Serie A with seven wins from 11 games. Sunday's opponents Frosinone are one of the surprise packages of the season so far and are just one place below the Rossoneri.

"We will have to wait until
items.text:
Paris Saint-Germain forward Désiré Doué was carried off on a stretcher with a serious knee injury late in the first half of the team's 3-2 win at Nice in Ligue 1 on Saturday.
The defending champions' 12th straight win in all competitions was soured by yet another injury.
"We will have to wait until tomorrow to know the exact nature of the injury. But it is a serious injury, we have seen the images," PSG coach Luis Enrique said after the game. "That's the life of a professional footballer, you have to realize that this is part of a career and you have to accept it."
It happened when he turned to shield the ball from Nice midfielder Sofiane Diop and his fully-extended leg buckled under him without any contact from Diop.
The France forward fell to the ground clutching his right knee in the 39th minute and looked in severe pain as he cried out. Moments later he was taken off on a stretcher and placed both hands on his face.
"He is sad and worried," Luis Enrique said. "He will come back twice as strong, I have no doubt."
The 21-year-old Doué -- who shot to prominence with an outstanding performance in the 2025 Champions League win against Inter Milan -- had scored his second league goal of the season earlier in the first half.
Spain forward Ferran Torres replaced him and scored the third goal. Senny Mayulu got PSG's opening goal.
Two-time defending champions PSG face Roma in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Doué missed stretches of last season with a calf strain and a thigh injury and had a bothersome ankle injury the previous season.
His latest injury is a concern for Enrique, after Khvicha Kvaratskhelia tore the ACL in his right knee against Barcelona on Oct. 20 and Ousmane Dembélé and captain Marquinhos tore thigh muscles in that game.
Dembélé came off the bench against Nice in the second half for PSG.
Information from The Associated Press contributed to this report.

items.text:
David Raya was forced off with an injury during Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle United on Saturday.
The Spain goalkeeper walked off holding his left arm and looked in discomfort as he did so. He was replaced by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
"Unfortunately, he had to come off which is never good news," Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta said. "He will get assessed now and he will probably have an MRI tomorrow to see what it is exactly because at the moment I don't know.
"It was a knock. I don't know how it happened or what the injury is at the moment so we'll have to see wait and see tomorrow.
"We know how important David is for us but tomorrow we will have more news."
The 31-year-old had played every minute of Arsenal's Premier League and Champions League games this season up to that point.
He also played 37 out of Arsenal's 38 games as they lifted the Premier League last season.
Raya has won the league's Golden Glove award in each of the last three seasons, and Arsenal have conceded the joint-fewest goals so far this Premier League season.
The Spaniard could join Bukayo Saka and Martín Zubimendi on the sidelines, although Saturday's game did see William Saliba feature in a Premier League squad for the first time this season.

He hopes his a
items.text:
Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
- Published
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.
At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.
He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.
"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.
But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.
Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.
The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.
His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.
Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).
Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.
The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.
In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".
His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.
But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.
"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.
The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.
Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.
But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.
Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.
But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.
Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.
"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.
The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.
Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.
Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.
Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.
This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.
But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.
Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.
"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.
Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.
For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.
Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.
The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.
Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.
The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.
The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; £56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.
Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.
These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.
Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.
The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.
Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.
"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

items.text:
Nigeria: At least 24 dead after boat capsizes
November 22, 2026
A boat capsized in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, the country's emergency agency said on Saturday.
"So far, 24 bodies have been recovered from the scene of the incident, while search and rescue operations are ongoing," said Manzo Ezekiel, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency.
The boat was carrying mourners for a burial ceremony from the town of Ayama to Ukubie in the southern Bayelsa State on Friday when it sank.
Boat reportedly suffered mechanical failure
Authorities have not confirmed how many passengers were on board.
"Those who lost their lives in the tragedy did not deserve to die that way," Nigerian President Bola Tinubu said in a statement on X.
Two children were among the four bodies initially recovered from the water on Friday, when 24 survivors were rescued, according to police.
Police spokesman Musa Mohammed said that preliminary reports suggested that the boat suffered a mechanical problem.
Deadly boat mishaps in Nigeria
Boat accidents are common on Nigeria's busy river networks. Overloading, poor vessel maintenance, and failure to comply with safety norms usually cause them.
In August, at least 51 died after a boat capsized in northwest Nigeria's Sokoto State.
In September 2025, a boat carrying over 100 passengers sank in north-central Niger State, leaving dozens dead.

items.title: Lebanese president demands Israel withdrawal, decries Iran’s interference
items.summary:
Lebanese president demands Israel withdrawal, decries Iran’s interference
Joseph Aoun says ‘two fundamental obstacles, inseparably linked’ mean Lebanon cannot fully celebrate its independence.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has decried Iran’s meddling in Lebanon’s affairs and demanded Israel’s withd
items.text:
Lebanese president demands Israel withdrawal, decries Iran’s interference
Joseph Aoun says ‘two fundamental obstacles, inseparably linked’ mean Lebanon cannot fully celebrate its independence.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has decried Iran’s meddling in Lebanon’s affairs and demanded Israel’s withdrawal from his country’s south.
In a speech on Saturday, on the eve of Lebanon’s 83rd independence anniversary, Aoun said Lebanon faces two interconnected fateful tests: the “Israeli occupation of parts of our land” and “foreign interference” from “some influential parties in the Iranian regime” through weapons and decisions outside the authority of the Lebanese state.
These “two fundamental obstacles, inseparably linked” mean that Lebanon cannot fully celebrate its independence, he added.
“Withdraw from every inch of Lebanese territory. Stop your attacks. And return our captives,” Aoun demanded of Israel.
Dozens of Lebanese citizens are believed to be held in Israeli detention centres, including civilians as well as members of the Hezbollah armed group captured during fighting in southern Lebanon.
The president also pledged to press ahead with plans to bring all weapons under state control, declaring that there would be “no weapons outside the state that take orders from, or serve the interests of foreign powers.”
“You must hand over your weapons,” Aoun said.
Lebanon’s government has promised to disarm Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese group whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and that has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel.
Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement in June, following US-mediated talks, which included the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanese territories and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
But implementation has stalled, with Hezbollah refusing to surrender its weapons and Israel continuing to strike Lebanon.
Israeli strikes
On Saturday, Israeli strikes hit the districts of Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil and Marjayoun in southern Lebanon.
Al Jazeera correspondents reported that one of the air strikes hit the outskirts of Baraachit, a town in Bint Jbeil.
They said Baraachit came under Israeli gunfire at dawn and reported the movement of Israeli military vehicles on the outskirts of the town.
Israeli warplanes launched a second missile attack on the town of Kfar Tebnit in Nabatieh, after the first failed to detonate, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA).
The NNA reported that Israeli forces carried out three explosions in Wadi al-Khiam in the Marjayoun district, but gave no further details.
Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon have killed at least 4,386 people and wounded 12,407 others since March 2, when the latest Hezbollah-Israel war started.
Lebanon’s Ministry of Health said that since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, Israeli strikes in Lebanon have killed 8,953 people and injured 30,643 others.
